why: Analysts are hired to tell signal from noise. Questions about averages, distributions and A/B tests are standard in data analyst interviews.
outcome: describe a dataset correctly, define good KPIs, explain uncertainty and read an A/B test result without common mistakes.

lessons.title: Describe data: centre, spread, distribution
text: Before any conclusion, look at the distribution: a histogram tells you more than a single average. Salaries, delivery times and revenues are usually skewed, with a long tail of high values.
With skewed data, the median and percentiles describe the 'typical' case better than the mean.
points: Mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is not.
Standard deviation measures spread around the mean; the interquartile range (P75 − P25) is robust.
Report percentiles for experiences people feel (P90 response time).
Correlation is not causation: a third factor can drive both.

example.code:
import pandas as pd
salaries = pd.Series([32000, 35000, 38000, 41000, 45000, 120000])
print(salaries.mean())    # 51833: pulled up by one outlier
print(salaries.median())  # 39500: closer to the typical salary
print(salaries.quantile([0.25, 0.75]))

lessons.title: KPIs and metrics that mean something
text: A good KPI is tied to a goal, clearly defined (numerator, denominator, period, filters), and moves when the business really changes.
Rates need their volumes: '50% conversion' on 4 visitors is not the same as on 40,000.
points: Write the definition: 'Application rate = applications / offer views, per week, excluding internal traffic'.
Pair a primary metric with guardrail metrics (e.g. conversion up, but refunds must not rise).
Beware of averages of ratios; compute the ratio of totals instead.
Segment results (device, country) before concluding, but watch for Simpson's paradox.

lessons.title: A/B tests and significance
text: An A/B test randomly splits users between the current version (A) and a change (B), then compares a metric. Randomisation is what lets you talk about causation.

The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if there were actually no effect. A small p-value (often < 0.05) means the result is unlikely to be pure noise; it does not measure how big or important the effect is.
points: Decide the metric, the minimum effect worth detecting and the sample size before starting.
Do not stop the test the moment it looks significant ('peeking' inflates false positives).
Report the effect with a confidence interval, e.g. +2.1 pts [+0.4; +3.8].
Check sample ratio mismatch: a 50/50 split that ends 46/54 signals a bug.

example.code:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest
# conversions and visitors for A and B
stat, p_value = proportions_ztest([410, 470], [10000, 10000])
print(round(p_value, 4))  # about 0.04 -> unlikely to be noise at the 5% level

lessons.title: Correlation, regression and classic traps
text: Correlation measures how two variables move together, from -1 to 1. A simple linear regression draws the best straight line through the points: its slope says how much y changes on average when x increases by one unit.

Correlation is not causation. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer: the hidden cause is the weather (a confounder). Other traps: a few outliers that create a correlation, averages that reverse when you split by group (Simpson's paradox), and testing so many metrics that one looks significant by chance.
points: Always plot the data before trusting r: very different shapes can share the same r.
r² is the share of the variance of y explained by the line.
To claim a cause, you need an experiment (A/B test) or a careful design that controls confounders.
Segment results (by country, device, new or returning users) before concluding.

example.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

ads = np.array([10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35])        # ad spend (k€)
sales = np.array([110, 135, 170, 180, 220, 240])  # sales (k€)

r, p = stats.pearsonr(ads, sales)
fit = stats.linregress(ads, sales)
print(f"r = {r:.2f}, slope = {fit.slope:.1f} k€ sales per k€ of ads")
# r = 0.99, slope = 5.2 -> strong association, not proof of cause
example.note: Strong correlation; the budget and the season may both drive sales.

lessons.title: Sampling and bias: who is in your data?
text: You almost never measure the whole population: you work on a sample (the customers who answered a survey, one month of logs, the users of the app). A sample is useful only if it resembles the population you want to talk about. The first question to ask about any dataset is therefore: how did these rows get here, and who is missing?

Two different problems hide behind 'the sample is not perfect'. Random error comes from chance: another random sample would give a slightly different number. It shrinks as the sample grows, but slowly: the standard error of a mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n, so you need four times more data to halve it. Bias is a systematic gap between the sample and the population, and more data does not reduce it at all; a biased sample of one million rows is just as wrong, only more confident.

Classic biases in business data: selection bias (only customers who opted in to tracking), non-response bias (satisfied customers rarely answer surveys, angry ones do), survivorship bias (studying only the companies or customers still active), and convenience samples (testing a feature on colleagues). Time also matters: a week of data in August or around Black Friday is not a typical week.

The protection is random sampling where you control the selection, stratified sampling when small groups must be represented (draw separately in each region or segment), and, when you cannot control it, an honest description of who is in the data and who is not.
points: Standard error of a mean = s / √n: four times the data halves the error.
More data reduces random error, never bias.
Ask who could not or would not appear in the data (churned customers, non-respondents, untracked users).
Stratify when you need reliable numbers for small segments.
Compare the sample with known totals (age, region, plan) to spot gaps.

example.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
# Population: 100,000 basket values, skewed like real revenue
population = rng.lognormal(mean=3.5, sigma=0.8, size=100_000)
print(round(population.mean(), 1))

for n in [100, 400, 1600]:
    means = [rng.choice(population, n).mean() for _ in range(1000)]
    print(n, round(np.std(means), 2))   # spread of the sample mean halves when n is x4

# Biased sample: bigger baskets are more likely to answer a survey
answered = population[rng.random(population.size) < population / population.max()]
print(len(answered), round(answered.mean(), 1))   # far above the true mean
example.note: The biased sample still has thousands of rows; its mean stays wrong however many you collect.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals in practice
text: A single number such as 'conversion is 4.2%' hides how precise it is. A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the true figure, for example 4.2% [3.5%; 5.0%]. The 95% refers to the method: if you repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true value. It does not cover bias in the data, only random error.

Three cases cover most analyst work. For a mean, use the t distribution with the standard error s / √n; with a few dozen observations or more it is close to mean ± 2 standard errors. For a proportion (conversion, churn, share of tickets), use the Wilson interval, which behaves well with small counts and rates near 0% or 100%. For a median, a percentile or any statistic without a simple formula, use the bootstrap: resample your data with replacement thousands of times, compute the statistic each time and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

Reading intervals well is half the skill. A wide interval means you do not know much yet, whatever the point estimate says. If two intervals do not overlap, the difference is significant; if they overlap a little, the difference may still be significant, so test the difference itself rather than eyeballing. And the width shrinks with √n, so reaching twice the precision costs four times the data.
For a business audience, state the range in plain words: 'between 3.5% and 5.0%, most likely around 4.2%'. Decisions should hold across the whole range, not only at the point estimate.
points: Mean: mean ± t × s / √n (scipy.stats.t.interval).
Proportion: Wilson interval (statsmodels proportion_confint, method="wilson").
Median or other statistics: bootstrap (scipy.stats.bootstrap).
Overlapping intervals do not prove 'no difference': test the difference.
Always show the n behind a rate and its interval.

example.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

basket = np.array([42, 55, 38, 61, 47, 52, 39, 70, 44, 58, 49, 63])
low, high = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=len(basket) - 1,
                             loc=basket.mean(), scale=stats.sem(basket))
print(f"mean {basket.mean():.1f}, 95% CI [{low:.1f}; {high:.1f}]")

low, high = proportion_confint(count=126, nobs=3000, alpha=0.05, method="wilson")
print(f"conversion 4.2%, 95% CI [{low:.1%}; {high:.1%}]")

res = stats.bootstrap((basket,), np.median, confidence_level=0.95)
print(res.confidence_interval)   # low and high for the median

lessons.title: Hypothesis tests and p-value pitfalls
text: A hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference could easily come from chance. You state a null hypothesis (no difference), compute a test statistic from the data and get a p-value: the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. The test you choose depends on the data, not on which one gives the smallest p-value.

Comparing the means of two independent groups (basket value in two regions, resolution time before and after a process change) calls for a t-test; use Welch's version (equal_var=False), which does not assume equal variances. When the same units are measured twice (the same agents before and after a training), use the paired t-test. With very skewed data and small samples, the Mann-Whitney test compares the groups without assuming normality. For counts in categories (contract type by job board, plan by country), use the chi-square test of independence on the contingency table.

Most mistakes are in the reading. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and p > 0.05 does not prove there is no effect: the sample may simply be too small. With a huge sample, tiny and useless differences become 'significant', so always report the effect size and its confidence interval next to the p-value. Finally, if you run 20 tests at the 5% level, you should expect one false positive by chance: correct for multiple comparisons (Holm or Bonferroni) or decide on one primary metric in advance.
Write the conclusion as a decision with its uncertainty, not as 'significant' or 'not significant' alone.
points: Two independent means: Welch t-test, stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False).
Same units twice: paired test, stats.ttest_rel.
Categories: chi-square, stats.chi2_contingency(table).
Report effect size + interval + p-value, never the p-value alone.
Many tests: statsmodels multipletests(pvals, method="holm").

example.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Ticket resolution time (hours) with the old and the new triage process
old = np.array([5.2, 6.1, 4.8, 7.3, 5.9, 6.5, 8.0, 5.5, 6.8, 7.1])
new = np.array([4.1, 5.0, 4.6, 5.8, 4.9, 5.2, 6.3, 4.4, 5.6, 5.1])
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(new, old, equal_var=False)   # Welch t-test
print(f"difference {new.mean() - old.mean():.2f} h, t = {t:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}")

# Contract type of applications on two job boards
table = np.array([[120, 80, 40],    # board A: permanent, fixed-term, freelance
                  [150, 60, 30]])   # board B
chi2, p, dof, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
print(f"chi2 = {chi2:.1f}, dof = {dof}, p = {p:.3f}")
example.note: Check that every expected count in 'expected' is at least 5 before trusting the chi-square result.

lessons.title: Designing an A/B test and communicating the result
text: Most failed A/B tests were lost before they started. Write a short plan first: the hypothesis, one primary metric, the guardrail metrics, the unit of randomisation (user, not page view, if the same person comes back), the minimum detectable effect (MDE) worth shipping, the significance level (usually 5%) and the power (usually 80%). These choices fix the sample size, and the sample size divided by the daily traffic gives the duration.

Sample size grows fast when the effect is small: halving the MDE needs about four times more users. If the required duration is unrealistic, test a bolder change, pick a more sensitive metric or accept that the test cannot answer the question. Run whole weeks so that weekdays and weekends are both represented.

Peeking is the classic trap: checking the p-value every day and stopping as soon as it drops below 0.05 can multiply the false positive rate several times. Either wait for the planned sample size or use a method built for continuous monitoring (sequential tests). Before reading the metric, check the sample ratio: if a 50/50 split ends 51/49 on 100,000 users, a chi-square test will flag it, and a mismatch usually means a bug in assignment or tracking that invalidates the result.

When you present the result, lead with the decision and the size of the effect, then the uncertainty: 'B increased conversion by 0.5 points, plausibly between 0.1 and 0.9; with 90,000 visitors a month that is roughly 90 to 810 extra orders; guardrails are flat; we recommend shipping.' Avoid the words 'proved' and 'no effect'; say 'we could not detect an effect larger than X'.
points: Plan before launch: metric, MDE, alpha, power, duration, guardrails.
Halving the MDE needs about four times the sample.
No peeking: wait for the planned size or use a sequential method.
Check sample ratio mismatch before reading results.
Translate the interval into business units (orders, euros) for decision makers.

example.code:
from scipy.stats import chisquare
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

baseline, target = 0.040, 0.045   # +0.5 pt is the smallest lift worth shipping
effect = proportion_effectsize(target, baseline)
n_per_group = NormalIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=effect, alpha=0.05,
                                           power=0.8, ratio=1)
print(round(n_per_group))   # about 25,500 users per group

# Sample ratio check on a planned 50/50 split
stat, p = chisquare([50_912, 49_088])
print(f"SRM p-value = {p:.1e}")   # far below 0.001: investigate before reading results
example.note: With 3,000 eligible users a day, 2 x 25,500 users take about 17 days: run 3 full weeks.

items: Trend reverses when groups are combined
No difference between A and B
Plausible range for the true effect
Chance to detect a real effect (aim 80%)
Minimum detectable effect, sets sample size
Systematic gap; more data does not fix it
Only the survivors are in the data
Method that captures the true value 95% of the time
Resample with replacement to get an interval
How big the difference is, beyond the p-value
Sample size for a given MDE and power
Split differs from plan: likely a bug
Stopping when p < 0.05 inflates false positives

pitfalls: Reporting the mean of a skewed distribution as 'typical'.
Stopping an A/B test early because it 'looks significant'.
Testing many metrics and only reporting the one that came out significant.
Concluding causation from a correlation in observational data.
Believing a bigger dataset removes bias: a million self-selected survey answers are still self-selected.
Reading p > 0.05 as 'no effect' when the test simply lacked the sample size to detect one.
Launching an A/B test without a planned sample size and duration, then stopping when the dashboard turns green.

exercises.q: Average delivery time is 3 days but customers complain. What would you look at?
exercises.answer: The distribution: median and P90/P95. A long tail (some deliveries taking 10+ days) can hide behind a good average. Then segment by region, carrier and product.

exercises.q: Variant B has 4.7% conversion vs 4.1% for A, p = 0.04, on 10,000 users each. What do you tell the product manager?
exercises.answer: B likely improves conversion: the difference is unlikely to be noise. The estimated lift is about +0.6 points, and the confidence interval should be shared because the true lift could be smaller. Check guardrail metrics and that the test ran its planned duration before rolling out.

exercises.q: Why compute a conversion rate as total conversions / total visitors rather than the average of daily rates?
exercises.answer: Days have different traffic. Averaging daily rates gives a small day the same weight as a big one, which biases the result. The ratio of totals weights every visitor equally.

exercises.q: A manager says: 'Customers who use our app spend 40% more, so pushing everyone to the app will raise revenue by 40%.' What is wrong, and how would you check?
exercises.hint: Who chooses to use the app?
exercises.answer: Self-selection: the most engaged customers choose the app, so they would spend more anyway; the app is correlated with spending, it does not prove it causes it. Check by comparing similar customers (same tenure, past spend) before and after adopting the app, or better, run an experiment that randomly encourages a group to use the app and compare its revenue with a control group.

exercises.q: A survey sent to all customers gets 8% responses and shows 92% satisfaction. The manager wants to publish '92% of our customers are satisfied'. What do you say?
exercises.answer: The figure describes respondents, not customers: non-response bias is likely because satisfied and unhappy customers do not answer at the same rate. Compare respondents with the customer base (tenure, plan, region, past complaints), report it as '92% of respondents', and if the number matters, survey a random sample with follow-ups to raise the response rate.

exercises.q: Out of 1,200 trial users, 180 converted to paid. Compute the conversion rate with a 95% Wilson confidence interval in Python.
exercises.answer:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

rate = 180 / 1200
low, high = proportion_confint(180, 1200, alpha=0.05, method="wilson")
print(f"{rate:.1%} [{low:.1%}; {high:.1%}]")

exercises.q: Two arrays, a and b, hold the order values of customers in two independent regions. Test whether the mean order value differs, without assuming equal variances.
exercises.answer:
from scipy import stats

t, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
print(f"diff = {a.mean() - b.mean():.2f}, p = {p:.4f}")

exercises.q: Baseline checkout conversion is 10%. The team wants to detect a lift to 11% with 80% power at the 5% level. Compute the users needed per group.
exercises.answer:
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

effect = proportion_effectsize(0.11, 0.10)
n = NormalIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=effect, alpha=0.05, power=0.8, ratio=1)
print(round(n))   # about 14,700 per group

interview.q: Explain a p-value to a non-technical person.
interview.a: If the change really had no effect, the p-value is how often we would still see a difference this big just by chance. A small value means chance alone is an unlikely explanation. It does not tell us how big or valuable the effect is.
Median, because salaries are skewed by a few very high values. The median describes the typical salary; I would add percentiles to show the spread.

interview.q: What can go wrong in an A/B test?
interview.a: Too small a sample, peeking and stopping early, multiple metrics without correction, sample ratio mismatch from a bug, novelty effects, and running it during an unusual period.

interview.q: How do you explain to a manager that correlation is not causation?
interview.a: With a concrete example from their data: the users who adopt a feature were already the most engaged, so they would spend more anyway. The feature and spending move together, but engagement drives both. To measure the real effect, we need an experiment where users are randomly given the feature, or at least a comparison of similar users before and after.

interview.q: What is the difference between random error and bias?
interview.a: Random error is the noise from working on a sample: another sample would give a slightly different value, and it shrinks as the sample grows. Bias is a systematic gap because the sample does not represent the population, for example only engaged users answering a survey. More data reduces random error but leaves bias untouched; you fix bias by changing how the data is collected or by adjusting for it.

interview.q: How do you interpret a 95% confidence interval?
interview.a: It is a range of plausible values for the true figure. If we repeated the study many times, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true value. In practice I read its width as our precision, and I check whether the decision would be the same at both ends of the interval.

interview.q: Your A/B test shows p = 0.30. The product manager concludes the feature has no effect. Do you agree?
interview.a: Not necessarily. A high p-value means we could not distinguish the effect from noise, not that the effect is zero. I look at the confidence interval: if it is narrow around zero, any effect is probably too small to matter; if it is wide, the test was underpowered and a meaningful effect is still possible. Then we decide whether a larger test is worth running.

interview.q: How do you decide how long an A/B test should run?
interview.a: From the sample size, which comes from the baseline rate, the minimum effect worth detecting, the significance level and the power. I divide that sample by the eligible daily traffic and round up to full weeks to cover weekly patterns. I fix the duration before launch and do not stop early because the result looks good.
